passage:
Dear Ujjwal,

You asked how the first month abroad is going, and I have a small funny story. In the lab corridor I wanted to call my lab partner over, so I did what we do at home: palm down, fingers scooping the air towards me. Nothing. He frowned, then came slowly with a puzzled look. Yesterday I saw a local student beckon someone with an upturned finger, and the person laughed and came straight over. Then in the canteen queue a staff member glanced at that same finger with a stiff face. So it isn't the same everywhere, even here.

I've decided to stop guessing. I use words now, "could you come?", and I watch what people do.

Miss you all. 🙂

Parveen

qa.q: What gesture did Parveen use to call the lab partner?
qa.a: Parveen used a palm-down scoop of the fingers towards the body.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling about the beckoning puzzle?
qa.a: Parveen was amused but a little unsure, since the gesture got a frown from one person and a laugh from another. Deciding to use words and watch others suggests Parveen wants to avoid causing offence.

qa.q: What could a student new to a country do about unfamiliar gestures?
qa.a: Use plain words to call people, watch what locals do, and ask a friendly classmate what a gesture means.

qa.q: How might the lab partner have seen the palm-down scoop?
qa.a: The lab partner frowned and came slowly with a puzzled look, so the scoop may have seemed unclear or odd rather than friendly.

grounding: A student abroad finds beckoning gestures mean different things and chooses to watch locals and use words.

passage: Imran, it's Usha, remember when I told you about my first term in Norway? The funniest part was the beckoning. In my first week I called a course-mate over with the palm-down scoop we use back home, and she just laughed and said it looked like I was sweeping crumbs. Another time I crooked one finger upwards at a boy at the bus stop, thinking it was very casual, and he raised his eyebrows and stepped back. I felt my ears go hot. My housemate said in some places that finger is rude, or at least bossy. So I started asking, "Is it okay if I call you like this?", and I copied the way the locals waved. Guessing from home habits was the mistake.

qa.a: Usha's first term was in Norway.

qa.q: How did Usha feel when the boy raised his eyebrows and stepped back?
qa.a: Usha felt embarrassed, shown by the ears going hot, and realised the crooked finger had landed badly. The boy's reaction may also have been plain surprise, so it is a cue rather than proof.

qa.q: What would you advise Usha to do in a new country when calling someone?
qa.a: Ask politely, use a word or a wave that locals use, and avoid assuming home gestures will carry the same meaning.

qa.q: What was it like for the course-mate when Usha used the scoop?
qa.a: The course-mate found it funny, and said it looked like sweeping crumbs, so the meaning simply didn't carry over.

grounding: A student abroad learns that a beckon friendly in one place is rude or odd in another, and that asking and watching is wiser.
